The ***Sumerian King List*** (abbreviated ***SKL***) or ***Chronicle of the One Monarchy*** is an ancient [literary composition](Composition_(language) "Composition (language)") written in [Sumerian](Sumerian_language "Sumerian language") that was likely created and redacted to legitimize the claims to power of various city-states and kingdoms in southern <Mesopotamia> during the late third and early second millennium BC.[[2]](Sumerian_King_List#cite_note-:9-2)[[3]](Sumerian_King_List#cite_note-:12-3)[[4]](Sumerian_King_List#cite_note-:11-4) It does so by repetitively listing [Sumerian](Sumer "Sumer") cities, the kings that ruled there, and the lengths of their reigns. Especially in the early part of the list, these reigns often span thousands of years. In the oldest known version, dated to the [Ur III period](Third_Dynasty_of_Ur "Third Dynasty of Ur") (c. (circa) 2112 – c. 2004 BC) but probably based on [Akkadian](Akkadian_Empire "Akkadian Empire") source material, the *SKL* reflected a more linear transition of power from [Kish](Kish_(Sumer) "Kish (Sumer)"), the first city to receive kingship, to [Akkad](Akkad_(city) "Akkad (city)"). In later versions from the [Old Babylonian period](Old_Babylonian_Empire "Old Babylonian Empire"), the list consisted of a large number of cities between which kingship was transferred, reflecting a more cyclical view of how kingship came to a city, only to be inevitably replaced by the next. In its best-known and best-preserved version, as recorded on the [Weld-Blundell Prism](Weld-Blundell_Prism "Weld-Blundell Prism"), the *SKL* begins with a number of [antediluvian](Antediluvian "Antediluvian") kings, who ruled before a flood swept over the land, after which kingship went to [Kish](Kish_(Sumer) "Kish (Sumer)"). It ends with a dynasty from <Isin> (early second millennium BC), which is well-known from other contemporary sources.

The *SKL* is preserved in several versions. Most of these date to the Old Babylonian period, but the oldest version dates to the Ur III period. The [clay tablets](Clay_tablet "Clay tablet") on which the *SKL* was recorded were generally found on sites in southern Mesopotamia. These versions differ in their exact content; some sections are missing, others are arranged in a different order, names of kings may be absent or the lengths of their reigns may vary. These differences are both the result of copying errors, and of deliberate editorial decisions to change the text to fit current needs.

In the past, the *Sumerian King List* was considered as an invaluable source for the reconstruction of the political history of [Early Dynastic Mesopotamia](Early_Dynastic_Period_(Mesopotamia) "Early Dynastic Period (Mesopotamia)"). More recent research has indicated that the use of the *SKL* is fraught with difficulties, and that it should only be used with caution, if at all, in the study of ancient Mesopotamia during the third and early second millennium BC.

**Eridu** ([Cuneiform](Sumerian_language "Sumerian language"): NUN.KI [𒉣](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/𒉣 "wikt:𒉣")[𒆠](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/𒆠 "wikt:𒆠"); [Sumerian](Sumerian_language "Sumerian language"): eridugki; [Akkadian](Akkadian_language "Akkadian language"): *irîtu*) was a Sumerian city located at **Tell Abu Shahrain** ([Arabic](Arabic_language "Arabic language"): تل أبو شهرين), also Abu Shahrein or Tell Abu Shahrayn, an [archaeological site](Archaeological_site "Archaeological site") in southern <Mesopotamia>. It is located in [Dhi Qar Governorate](Dhi_Qar_Governorate "Dhi Qar Governorate"), <Iraq> near the modern city of <Basra>. Eridu is traditionally believed to be the earliest city in southern Mesopotamia based on the Sumerian King List. Located 12 kilometers southwest of the ancient site of <Ur>, Eridu was the southernmost of a conglomeration of [Sumerian](Sumer "Sumer") cities that grew around temples, almost in sight of one another. The city gods of Eridu were <Enki> and his consort <Damkina>. Enki, later known as Ea, was considered to have founded the city. His temple was called E-Abzu, as Enki was believed to live in <Abzu>, an aquifer from which all life was believed to stem. According to Sumerian temple hymns another name for the temple of Ea/Enki was called Esira (Esirra).
> "... The temple is constructed with gold and lapis lazuli, Its foundation on the nether-sea (apsu) is filled in. By the river of Sippar (Euphrates) it stands. O Apsu pure place of propriety, Esira, may thy king stand within thee. ..."[[1]](Eridu#cite_note-1)[[2]](Eridu#cite_note-2)

At nearby Ur there was a temple of Ishtar of Eridu (built by Lagash ruler <Ur-Baba>) and a sanctuary of Inanna of Eridu (built by Ur III ruler <Ur-Nammu>). Ur-Nammu also recorded building a temple of Ishtar of Eridu at Ur which is assume to have been a rebuild.[[3]](Eridu#cite_note-3)[[4]](Eridu#cite_note-4)

One of the religious quarters of <Babylon>, containing the Esagil temple and the temple of <Annunitum> among others, was also named Eridu.[[5]](Eridu#cite_note-5)

## History

Eridu is one of the earliest settlements in the region, founded c. (circa) 5400 BC during the Early Ubaid period, at that time close to the [Persian Gulf](Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf") near the mouth of the <Euphrates> River though in modern times about 90 miles inland. Excavation has shown that the city was founded on a virgin sand-dune site with no previous habitation. With possible breaks in occupation in the Early Dynastic III and Akkadian Empire periods the city was inhabited up to the <Neo-Babylonian> though in later times it was primarily a cultic site. According to the excavators, construction of the Ur III ziggurat and associated buildings was preceded by the destruction of preceding construction and its use as leveling fill so no remains from that time were found. At a small mound 1 kilometer north of Eridu two Early Dynastic III palaces were found, with an enclosure wall. **Bad-tibira** ([Sumerian](Sumerian_language "Sumerian language"): 𒂦𒁾𒉄𒆠, bad3-tibiraki), "Wall of the Copper Worker(s)",[[1]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-1) or "Fortress of the Smiths",[[2]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-2) identified as modern **Tell al-Madineh** (also Tell Madineh), between [Ash Shatrah](Ash_Shatrah "Ash Shatrah") and Tell as-Senkereh (ancient <Larsa>) and 33 kilometers northeast of ancient <Girsu> in southern <Iraq>,[[3]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-3) was an ancient [Sumerian](Sumer "Sumer") city on the Iturungal canal (built by Ur III ruler <Ur-Nammu>), which appears among [antediluvian](Antediluvian "Antediluvian") cities in the [Sumerian King List](Sumerian_King_List "Sumerian King List"). Its Akkadian name was **Dûr-gurgurri**.[[4]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-4) It was also called Παντιβίβλος (**Pantibiblos**) by Greek authors such as <Berossus>, transmitted by <Abydenus> and [Apollodorus](Apollodorus_of_Athens "Apollodorus of Athens"). This may reflect another version of the city's name, **Patibira**, "Canal of the Smiths".[[5]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-5)

There is known to be a temple of the deity <Kittum> at Bad-tibira.[[6]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-6) It has been suggested that Ninsheshegarra, an aspect of the goddess <Geshtinanna> who is sister of <Dumuzid>, was worshiped in the temple Esheshegarra at Bad-tibira.[[7]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-7)[[8]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-8)

## Bad-tibira in Sumerian literature

According to the *[Sumerian King List](Sumerian_King_List "Sumerian King List")*, Bad-tibira was the second city to "exercise kingship" in Sumer before the flood, following <Eridu>. These kings were said to be <En-men-lu-ana>, <En-men-gal-ana> and [Dumuzid the Shepherd](Dumuzid_the_Shepherd "Dumuzid the Shepherd").

The early Sumerian text *<Inanna>'s [descent to the netherworld](Descent_to_the_Underworld "Descent to the Underworld")* mentions the city's temple, [E](E_(temple) "E (temple)")-mush-kalamma(a temple to <Lulal> ). In this tale, Inanna dissuades demons from the netherworld from taking <Lulal>, patron of Bad-tibira, who was living in squalor. They eventually take Dumuzid, who lived in palatial opulence at <Uruk>. This Dumuzid is called "the Shepherd",[[9]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-9) who on the King List resides at Bad-Tibira in contrast to the post-diluvian [Dumuzid, the Fisherman](Dumuzid%2C_the_Fisherman "Dumuzid, the Fisherman"), who reigns in Uruk.

> "For the goddess Inanna, [la]dy of Eanna, his lady, Ur-Nammu, mighty man, king of Ur, king of the lands of Sumer and Akkad, dug for her the Iturungal canal, her beloved canal"[[10]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-10)

The "brotherhood text" in [cuneiform](Cuneiform "Cuneiform") inscriptions on a cone, of which there are many exemplars, from the site records the friendship pact of <Entemena>, governor of <Lagash>, and <Lugal-kinishedudu>, governor of Uruk. It identifies Entemena as the builder of the temple E-mush[[11]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-11) to Inanna and Dumuzid, under his local epithet <Lugal>-E-mush.[[12]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-12)
> "For the goddess Inanna and the god Lugal-emush, En-metena, ruler of Lagash,
> Built the E-mush (“House — Radiance [of the Land]”), their beloved temple, and ordered (these) clay nails(?) for them. En-metena, who built the E-mush temple — is personal god is the god Sul-MUS×PA. At that time En-metena, ruler of Lagash, and Lugal-kinishe-dudu, ruler of Uruk, established a brotherhood (pact) (between themselves)."[[13]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-Frayne2008-13)

A foundation tablet of En-metena from the site, with multiple exemplars, also mentioned the building of E-Mush "... At that time, En-metena built for Lugalemush, the E-mush (“House — Radiance [of the Land]”) of Pa-tibira, his beloved temple, restoring it. ...". Pa-tibira appear to be an alternate spelling of Bad-tibira.[[13]](Bad-tibira#cite_note-Frayne2008-13)

**Sippar** ([Sumerian](Sumerian_language "Sumerian language"): 𒌓𒄒𒉣𒆠, **Zimbir**) was an [ancient Near Eastern](Ancient_Near_Eastern "Ancient Near Eastern") [Sumerian](Sumer "Sumer") and later [Babylonian](Babylonia "Babylonia") city on the east bank of the <Euphrates> river. Its *[tell](Tell_(archaeology) "Tell (archaeology)")* is located at the site of modern **Tell Abu Habbah** near <Yusufiyah> in <Iraq>'s [Baghdad Governorate](Baghdad_Governorate "Baghdad Governorate"), some 69 km (43 mi) north of <Babylon> and 30 km (19 mi) southwest of <Baghdad>. The city's ancient name, Sippar, could also refer to its sister city, <Sippar-Amnanum> (located at the modern site of Tell ed-Der); a more specific designation for the city here referred to as Sippar was Sippar-Yahrurum.[[1]](Sippar#cite_note-1)

## History

Despite the fact that thousands of cuneiform [clay tablets](Clay_tablet "Clay tablet") have been recovered at the site, relatively little is known about the history of Sippar. As was often the case in Mesopotamia, it was part of a pair of cities, separated by a river. Sippar was on the east side of the Euphrates, while its sister city, Sippar-Amnanum (modern Tell ed-Der), was on the west.

While pottery finds indicate that the site of Sippar was in use as early as the [Uruk period](Uruk_period "Uruk period"), substantial occupation occurred only in the [Early Dynastic Period](Early_Dynastic_Period_(Mesopotamia) "Early Dynastic Period (Mesopotamia)") of the 3rd millennium BC, the [Old Babylonian](First_Babylonian_dynasty "First Babylonian dynasty") period of the 2nd millennium BC, and the <Neo-Babylonian> time of the 1st millennium BC. Lesser levels of use continued into the time of the [Achaemenid](Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire"), [Seleucid](Seleucid_Empire "Seleucid Empire") and [Parthian Empires](Parthian_Empire "Parthian Empire").[[2]](Sippar#cite_note-2)

Sippar was the cult site of the sun god (Sumerian <Utu>, Akkadian <Shamash>) and the home of his temple [E](%C3%89_(temple) "É (temple)")-babbara ([𒂍](%C3%89_(temple) "É (temple)")𒌓𒌓𒊏, means "white house").

During early Babylonian dynasties, Sippar was the production center of wool. The [Code of Hammurabi](Code_of_Hammurabi "Code of Hammurabi") stele was probably erected at Sippar. <Shamash> was the god of justice, and he is depicted handing authority to the king in the image at the top of the stele.[[3]](Sippar#cite_note-3) A closely related motif occurs on some cylinder seals of the [Old Babylonian](First_Babylonian_dynasty "First Babylonian dynasty") period.[[4]](Sippar#cite_note-4) By the end of the 19th century BC, Sippar was producing some of the finest [Old Babylonian](Akkadian_language "Akkadian language") cylinder seals.[[5]](Sippar#cite_note-5)

Sippar has been suggested as the location of the Biblical <Sepharvaim> in the [Old Testament](Old_Testament "Old Testament"), which alludes to the two parts of the city in its [dual](Dual_(grammatical_number) "Dual (grammatical number)") form.[[6]](Sippar#cite_note-6)

### Rulers

In the [Sumerian king list](Sumerian_king_list "Sumerian king list") a king of Sippar, <En-men-dur-ana>, is listed as one of the early pre-dynastic rulers of the region but has not yet turned up in the epigraphic records.

In his 29th year of reign <Sumu-la-El> of <Babylon> reported building the city wall of Sippar. Some years later <Hammurabi> of Babylon reported laying the foundations of the city wall of Sippar in his 23rd year and worked on the wall again in his 43rd year. His successor in Babylon, <Samsu-iluna> worked on Sippar's wall in his 1st year. The city walls, being typically made of mud bricks, required much attention. Records of [Nebuchadnezzar II](Nebuchadnezzar_II "Nebuchadnezzar II") and <Nabonidos> record that they repaired the Shamash temple E-babbara.

### Classical speculation

[Xisuthros](Ziusudra "Ziusudra"), the "Chaldean Noah" in Sumerian mythology, is said by <Berossus> to have buried the records of the [antediluvian](Antediluvian "Antediluvian") world here—possibly because the name of Sippar was supposed to be connected with *sipru*, "a writing".[[7]](Sippar#cite_note-7) And according to <Abydenus>, [Nebuchadnezzar II](Nebuchadnezzar_II "Nebuchadnezzar II") excavated a great reservoir in the neighbourhood.[[8]](Sippar#cite_note-8)

**Shuruppak** ([Sumerian](Sumerian_language "Sumerian language"): 𒋢𒆳𒊒𒆠 **Šuruppag*[KI](KI_(cuneiform) "KI (cuneiform)")*, "the healing place"), modern **Tell Fara**, was an ancient [Sumerian](Sumer "Sumer") city situated about 55 kilometres (35 mi) south of <Nippur> and 30 kilometers north of ancient <Uruk> on the banks of the <Euphrates> in <Iraq>'s [Al-Qādisiyyah Governorate](Al-Q%C4%81disiyyah_Governorate "Al-Qādisiyyah Governorate"). Shuruppak was dedicated to <Ninlil>, also called Sud, the goddess of grain and the air.[[1]](Shuruppak#cite_note-Jacobsen1987-1)

The city expanded to its greatest extent at the end of the Early Dynastic III period (2600 BC to 2350 BC) when it covered about 100 hectares.[[2]](Shuruppak#cite_note-2)

"Shuruppak" is sometimes also the name of a king of the city, legendary survivor of [the Flood](Flood_story "Flood story"), and supposed author of the [Instructions of Shuruppak](Instructions_of_Shuruppak "Instructions of Shuruppak")".

## Archaeology

Tell Fara extends about a kilometer from north to south. The total area is about 120 hectares, with about 35 hectares of the mound being more than 3 meters above the surrounding plain, with a maximum of 9 meters. The site consists of two mounds, one larger than the other, separated by an old canal bed as well as a lower town. It was visited by [William Loftus](William_Loftus_(archaeologist) "William Loftus (archaeologist)") in 1850. [Hermann Volrath Hilprecht](Hermann_Volrath_Hilprecht "Hermann Volrath Hilprecht") conducted a brief survey in 1900. He found "copper goatheads; a copper, pre-Sargonid sword; a lamp in the shape of a bird; a very archaic seal cylinder; a number of
pre-Sargonid tablets, and 60 incised plates of mother of pearl".[[3]](Shuruppak#cite_note-:0-3) It was first excavated between 1902 and 1903 by Walter Andrae, [Robert Koldewey](Robert_Koldewey "Robert Koldewey") and [Friedrich Delitzsch](Friedrich_Delitzsch "Friedrich Delitzsch") of the [German Oriental Society](Deutsche_Orient-Gesellschaft "Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft") for eight months. They used a new "modern" system which involved excavating trenches 8 feet wide and 5 feet deep every few yards running across the entire width of the larger mound. If a building wall was found in a trench it was further explored. Preliminary identification of the site as Suruppak came from a Ur III period clay nail which mentioned "Haladda, son of Dada, the patesi of Shuruppak (written SU.KUR.RUki)
repaired the ADUS of the Great Gate of the god Shuruppak (written dSU.KUR.RU-da)". Among other finds, roughly 1000 cuneiform tablets of [Early Dynastic](Early_Dynastic_Period_(Mesopotamia) "Early Dynastic Period (Mesopotamia)") III period were collected, which ended up in the Berlin Museum and the Istanbul Museum. [[4]](Shuruppak#cite_note-4) About a thousand Early Dynastic clay sealings and fragments (used to secure doors and containers) were also found. Most from cylinder seals but 19 were from stamp seals.[[5]](Shuruppak#cite_note-5) In 1903 the site was visited by [Edgar James Banks](Edgar_James_Banks "Edgar James Banks") who was excavating at the site of [Adab](Adab_(city) "Adab (city)"), a four hour walk to the north. Banks took photographs of the German trenches and noted a 20 foot in diameter well, constructed with plano-convex bricks, in the center of the larger mound as well as an arched sewer, similarly constructed. The latter was where tablets were found. Banks also noted that the smaller mound held a cemetery.[[6]](Shuruppak#cite_note-6)

Based on my research, I can now provide you with a comprehensive answer about the five cities from the world's oldest civilization (Sumer) that first exercised kingship according to the Sumerian King List.

## The Five Cities of First Kingship in Sumer

According to the **Sumerian King List** (an ancient cuneiform text from circa 2900-1792 BC), the five cities that first received or "exercised" kingship in the pre-diluvian era (before the great flood) were:

### 1. **Eridu**
- **Modern Location**: Tell Abu Shahrain, Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq
- **Geographic Details**: Located approximately 12 kilometers southwest of the ancient site of Ur, about 90 miles inland from the Persian Gulf (though much closer to the coast in ancient times)
- **Coordinates**: 30°48′57″N 45°59′46″E
- **Founded**: c. 5400 BC

### 2. **Bad-tibira**
- **Modern Location**: Tell al-Madineh (also called Tell Madineh), Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq
- **Geographic Details**: Located between Ash Shatrah and Tell as-Senkereh (ancient Larsa), approximately 33 kilometers northeast of ancient Girsu
- **Coordinates**: 31°22′47″N 45°59′59″E
- **Meaning**: "Wall of the Copper Worker(s)" or "Fortress of the Smiths"

### 3. **Larak**
- **Modern Location**: Not yet archaeologically identified
- **Geographic Details**: Scholars suggest a location to the east of Kish and near Isin in central Iraq
- **Patron Deity**: Pabilsag (a Ninurta-like warrior god)
- **Note**: This city remains unidentified at any specific archaeological site

### 4. **Sippar**
- **Modern Location**: Tell Abu Habbah, Baghdad Governorate, Iraq
- **Geographic Details**: Located approximately 69 km north of Babylon and 30 km southwest of Baghdad, on the east bank of the Euphrates river
- **Coordinates**: 33°03′32″N 44°15′08″E
- **Significance**: Cult site of the sun god Utu/Shamash

### 5. **Shuruppak**
- **Modern Location**: Tell Fara, Al-Qādisiyyah Governorate, Iraq
- **Geographic Details**: Located about 55 kilometers south of Nippur and 30 kilometers north of ancient Uruk, on the banks of the Euphrates
- **Coordinates**: 31°46′39″N 45°30′35″E
- **Patron Deity**: Ninlil (goddess of grain and air)
- **Founded**: c. 2600 BC (greatest extent reached during Early Dynastic III period)

---

## Summary Geographic Information

**All five cities are located in modern-day Iraq**, in the region historically known as **Sumer** in southern Mesopotamia. This area lies between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, along the fertile valley known as the "Cradle of Civilization." The civilization of Sumer is widely recognized as the **world's oldest known civilization**, emerging during the Chalcolithic and early Bronze Ages between the 6th and 5th millennium BC.

The Sumerian King List records these cities as exercising kingship before a great flood, with kings ruling for extraordinarily long periods (thousands of years each), before kingship descended upon Kish after the deluge.
